analysis.one_liner: Requires testing school drinking water for lead, quick notification of results, and grants to replace lead pipes.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its referral to the House Energy and Commerce Committee; it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the EPA to set a lead action level for school and day care drinking water, required public water systems to test water at schools the EPA flags as at-risk, and required those systems to notify the school district, local health agencies, the town, and the state within five business days if lead reached the action level. It would also create an EPA grant program to pay for testing and for replacing lead pipes and plumbing fixtures in schools, with results posted publicly and parents and staff notified. The bill never got a committee hearing or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Children who attend schools and day care facilities, especially in older buildings where lead service lines and plumbing are common, along with their parents and school staff. The bill benefits them by finding contaminated taps and funding replacement of lead plumbing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children in schools and day cares

how_it_helps.text: Requires public water systems to test for lead at schools the EPA identifies as at-risk, and to tell the school district, local health agencies, the municipality, and the state within five business days when lead meets or exceeds the action level, so contamination is not kept quiet.
Creates a grant program to pay for testing school drinking water and for replacing lead pipes, fittings, and fixtures with lead-free material, covering costs that schools otherwise could not afford.
Requires schools receiving grant funds to post test results publicly online and notify parent, teacher, and employee organizations.

analysis.who_pays: Public water utilities bear the cost of sampling and notification, and the federal Treasury pays for the grant program. Plumbing contractors and testing labs gain business from the mandated work.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets the lead action level at 'not less than' the general drinking water action level rather than a stricter school-specific standard, so it may not go beyond the existing 15 parts per billion benchmark unless EPA chose to tighten it.

The mandate falls on public water systems to sample and notify, an unfunded compliance cost for utilities, while the grant program requires annual federal appropriations that Congress would have to approve each year.
The bill addresses only schools and day care facilities, leaving lead risks in other older buildings untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: lead in drinking water harms children's development, and many schools cannot afford testing or pipe replacement on their own. The main costs are modest utility compliance work and federal grant spending, and the notification rules only add transparency. A fair criticism is that the bill did not set a stricter lead standard for schools than the general one, but the testing, funding, and disclosure requirements are a clear net benefit for families.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brenda Lawrence introduced the bill on September 27, 2018, with 48 original cosponsors, all Democrats, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The committee took no further action; the bill's only actions are its introduction and referral, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

The CRS summary shows the bill would have required EPA to write a school drinking water rule, required water systems to test and notify officials within five business days of high lead results, and created grants for testing and pipe replacement.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public water utilities avoided new testing and notification duties, and no federal money was appropriated for school lead pipe replacement. Children in schools with lead plumbing gained nothing because the program was never created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Water utilities; school kids gained nothing

against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral; never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote, so the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 49 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support, and the Republican-led committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have required utilities to sample school water and report high lead results to officials within five business days. Utilities had an interest in avoiding that new testing and disclosure burden, which the bill's death left unimposed.

The grant program would have funded replacing lead pipes, fittings, and fixtures with lead-free material, creating paid work for the plumbing and contracting trades. That interest is aligned with children's health since the work itself removes lead from schools.
Mandatory lead sampling at schools nationwide would have created a large new testing market for accredited labs, paid through the grants.
